style: Say firmly but kindly, like the clerk calling a hearing to order.
lines: Welcome to the Usage Panel. You are the chair. Tap a panelist to hear their case.
When you have heard enough, tap Acceptable, Acceptable in casual use only, or Not acceptable.
This is the record. Drag the Year slider, or tap Play the record, and watch the rulings change.
Now rule. Pick Accept, Accept with a note or Avoid for each setting, and the usage note writes itself.
Singular they. Can one person, or anyone at all, be they?
Literally. Can a word that means exactly also mean the opposite?
Hopefully. Can it mean I hope, at the start of a sentence?
The split infinitive. Is it wrong to put a word between to and its verb?
Less or fewer. Does ten items or less break a rule, and whose rule is it?
That is the record so far. Tap Your ruling to add your panel to it.
Your usage note is ready. Edit it in the box, or tap Copy note.
We use the pronoun a person uses; the open question here is the generic use. Tap Next sentence to return to that question.
Many readers were taught that they must be plural. If a sentence makes them stop and wonder, it costs us. I rewrite when I can, and I allow it when rewriting is clumsy.
Speakers have used they for one unknown person since around 1300. Shakespeare and Austen did it. A rule that most fluent speakers break every day is describing a style, not the language.
He or she is clunky, and alternating he and she confuses readers. Generic they is clear. I want students to know some readers still object, so I teach both.
He or she breaks the rhythm of a sentence. They keeps it moving and includes everyone.
Our readers range widely. I use it for anyone or a person, but I would rather name the person or make the subject plural.
Literally is the one word that promises no exaggeration. If it can also mean the opposite, I lose a tool. I cut it from formal copy.
Dickens, Twain and Fitzgerald all used it to intensify. Merriam-Webster lists the sense, and its usage guide calls it hyperbole, not a mistake.
In an essay it usually adds nothing and can make a reader laugh at the wrong moment. Cut it and the sentence gets stronger.
Gatsby literally glowed is a great line. Overstatement is a figure of speech, and this is how you mark it.
A reader might take it at its word. In news, literally should mean literally.
Who is doing the hoping? The sentence does not say. I write we hope, which is clearer.
The use goes back to at least 1648. Nobody objects to frankly or mercifully at the start of a sentence. The objection started in the 1960s.
Students hear this one argued about in class. I tell them it is accepted now, and that some graders still circle it.
There is no single word that does its job. It sounds natural, which is the point.
AP accepted it in 2012. It is fine in our pages.
Many readers still notice it. When the adverb can move without harm, I move it.
Writers split infinitives in the 1200s and 1300s. The rule against it first appeared in print in the 1800s, with no reason older than taste.
Try sentence (b) unsplit. To double more than our members? The split is the only clear version. Clarity wins.
Sometimes the adverb belongs right against the verb, for the beat.
Readers do not complain about it any more than they complain about commas. If it reads cleanly, it stays.
Fewer for things you count, less for amounts. It is a clean rule and readers expect it.
Less with countable nouns goes back to King Alfred in 888. The rule began in 1770 as one writer's personal preference.
Students lose points for this on tests. Know the rule, then decide when it matters.
Ten items or fewer is clunky on a sign. Less is shorter and sounds better.
Less people sounds wrong to many of our readers. I use fewer in copy.
